hook.text: Cut one cent per unit per month. After a year, that's twelve cents—multiplied by millions of units.

buildup.text: Kaizen costing pursues continuous, incremental cost reductions during the production phase.

discovery.text: Workers on the floor suggest small improvements—a better layout, fewer steps, less waste.

twist.text: No single change is dramatic, but compounded over years, the savings are enormous.

climax.text: Toyota and other Japanese firms built global dominance partly through relentless kaizen discipline.

punchline.text: Small daily improvements add up to massive yearly savings.

quiz.question: What is the core idea of kaizen costing?
options: Continuous small cost reductions over time

details.summary: Kaizen costing applies the Japanese philosophy of continuous improvement to cost reduction during the manufacturing process. Unlike target costing which sets goals before production, Kaizen costing aims for ongoing incremental cost reductions after production begins.
details.whyItMatters: Cost reduction doesn't stop at the design phase. Kaizen costing engages frontline workers in finding small, continuous savings that compound into significant competitive advantages over time.
takeaways: Kaizen costing sets cost reduction targets for each production period, not just at product launch
Small, continuous improvements accumulate into substantial savings over months and years
Workers on the production floor are the primary source of improvement ideas in Kaizen systems

faq.question: What is Kaizen costing?
faq.answer: Kaizen costing is a cost management approach that sets incremental cost reduction targets during the manufacturing phase. Rather than accepting current costs, it challenges every production period to find small improvements that reduce costs below the previous period's level.

faq.question: How is Kaizen costing different from target costing?
faq.answer: Target costing sets a cost goal during the product design phase before production begins. Kaizen costing picks up where target costing leaves off, driving ongoing cost reductions during actual production through continuous small improvements by frontline workers.
